name: Trichloroacetic acid peel

card.summary: A medium-depth clinical peel acid studied in small trials for photodamage, melasma and acne, with real burn and scarring risk.
card.note: Medium peels are performed by medical providers; risks include scarring and pigment change.

quick.overview:
TCA peels use trichloroacetic acid to injure and renew the skin and are classed as medium-depth. They are used by clinicians for photodamage, pigment problems, acne and scars.

Published human studies exist but are mostly small.
quick.mechanism: TCA is a strong acid that precipitates skin proteins, causing controlled injury; depth depends on concentration and technique.
quick.risks: ECHA lists severe skin burns and eye damage. Peel complications include prolonged redness, pigment changes, scarring and thinning. Wikipedia says medium peels must be done by a medical provider.

lead: A trichloroacetic acid (TCA) peel is a chemical peel that applies TCA, a strong acid, to the face or body to cause controlled injury and shedding of the skin. It is classed as a medium-depth peel and is performed by a medical provider in an office or outpatient setting. [1][2]

People use it to improve how skin looks: smoothing texture and fine lines in sun-damaged skin, lightening pigment such as melasma and sun spots, softening superficial acne scars and treating precancerous actinic keratoses. As the treated skin sheds, new skin forms, which is the route from peel to a more even, smoother surface. [3][4][5][14]

A related technique, TCA CROSS (chemical reconstruction of skin scars), places a high-concentration TCA solution into individual atrophic acne scars rather than across the whole face. A 2026 review of 34 publications covering 937 patients reported improvement rates of 50 to 80 percent, with more sessions giving more improvement and higher concentrations carrying more complication risk.[20]

Published trials are mostly small and compare TCA with other peels, ascorbic acid combinations or photodynamic therapy. Reported risks include pigment change, scarring and prolonged redness, and the European Chemicals Agency classes the chemical as causing severe skin burns and eye damage. [1][2][4][5][6]

angle.text: TCA peels are used by clinicians to resurface sun-damaged or pigmented skin and superficial scars. The visible change comes as the treated layers shed and renewed skin replaces them.

paras: TCA is a strong acid (pKa 0.66) that precipitates proteins and has been used in chemical peels, tattoo removal and wart treatment. [1] A peel produces a controlled injury so that the skin peels, which can reduce fine lines, acne scars and pigment. Wikipedia states that medium-depth peels must be done by a medical provider, that patients typically feel warmth or burning, and that a sedative or oral pain reliever may be used. [2]

Depth and effect vary with concentration and technique. Practitioners have developed combinations that make penetration more predictable: one 1994 paper describes glycolic acid before 35% TCA, and Monheit's Jessner's-TCA peel uses degreasing and a Jessner's pretreatment to let 35% TCA penetrate more evenly. [8][12] Obagi's modified TCA peel is described as a controlled variable-depth approach in which clinical signs during the peel were compared with histology. [13]

TCA was discovered in 1839 by the French chemist Jean-Baptiste Dumas. [1] Chemical peeling for skin resurfacing dates to the second half of the 19th century, when Austrian dermatologist Ferdinand von Hebra used agents such as phenol and nitric acid; Baker and Gordon popularised phenol-croton oil peels in the 1960s. [2] TCA became widely used as a medium-depth alternative, with refinements such as the glycolic-TCA peel (1994) and Jessner's-TCA peel (1995) described in the dermatology literature. [8][12]

Cosmetic and dermatologic uses studied include photodamage, melasma, acne and acne scars, and benign pigmented lesions in darker-skinned patients. [4][6][9][14] Medical uses include actinic keratoses and skin cancer prophylaxis, and molluscum contagiosum in immunocompromised patients. [3][5][10]

A systematic review of peels as single agents for melasma in darker skin pooled ten randomised trials and three prospective studies (478 patients) and found glycolic acid favoured over TCA on the MASI score, while other comparisons were not statistically different. [15]

Peels are done by clinicians in sessions, with the skin typically prepared beforehand and followed by a period of redness, frosting and shedding. Patients are generally advised by clinics to use sun protection during healing. TCA is also used in focal applications to individual pigmented spots. [9]

The European Chemicals Agency says TCA causes severe skin burns and eye damage. [1] Wikipedia lists photosensitivity, prolonged redness, hyperpigmentation, milia, skin thinning and texture changes among peel complications, and notes that both professional peels and low-strength home kits have caused injury and scarring. [2] One case report describes rapid development of keratoacanthomas after a body peel. [16]

sections.h: Peel depth and where TCA fits
paras: Chemical peels are commonly grouped by how deeply they act. Alpha hydroxy acids such as glycolic and lactic acid and the beta hydroxy acid salicylic acid are described as light peels, while phenol-croton oil formulations are the deep end of the range; TCA sits in the middle as the classic medium-depth agent. [2] Retinoic acid peels, often applied after a Jessner's solution pretreatment, are described as sitting between the light and medium categories. [2]

Because TCA has no anaesthetic effect of its own, patients typically report a warm or burning sensation during application, and clinics may offer an oral pain reliever or a mild sedative such as diazepam; many procedures are done without anaesthesia. [2] Treatment is delivered in an office or ambulatory surgery setting, and the source describes medium-depth peels as procedures that must be performed by a medical provider. [2]

Frosting, a whitening of the skin that appears as the acid coagulates proteins, is used by clinicians as a visual marker of how deeply a medium peel has acted; Obagi's modified TCA peel, studied in 1996, correlated such clinical signs with histology to make depth more predictable. [13]

Trichloroacetic acid is an organochlorine relative of acetic acid in which the three methyl hydrogens are replaced by chlorine, giving a colourless crystalline solid that dissolves very readily in water and is a far stronger acid than acetic acid (pKa 0.66). [1] It is produced by chlorinating acetic acid, and in laboratories it is widely used to precipitate proteins, DNA and RNA from solution, the same protein-coagulating property that underlies its skin effect. [1]

Beyond peels, TCA is used by clinicians to chemically destroy warts, including genital warts, and the same source notes it is regarded as acceptable for this use during pregnancy. [1] Industrially, its sodium salt was sold as a herbicide in the 1950s before heavy regulation. [1] The IARC classifies TCA in Group 2B, and the European Chemicals Agency lists the pure chemical as causing severe skin burns and eye damage and being very toxic to aquatic life. [1]

Reported after-effects of a medium peel include redness, a tight feeling, darkening and flaking of the skin, and then shedding over several days, with new skin underneath. Wikipedia lists photosensitivity and prolonged redness among recognised complications, and clinics generally advise sun protection while the skin heals. [2]

Interest in stronger acids has spread in online skin-care communities, where some members describe applying TCA to acne scars or pigment themselves. Wikipedia notes that both professional peels and low-concentration home kits have caused skin injury and scarring, and that medium-depth peels are intended to be performed by medical providers. [2] Practitioners who write about the topic generally frame depth control and skin type, particularly in darker skin where pigment change is a recognised risk, as the main variables. [15][9]

Acne scars are mostly atrophic, about 75 percent according to Wikipedia, and are described as ice-pick (narrow and deep), boxcar (sharp-edged, roughly 1.5 to 4 mm) and rolling (broader, wave-like) types.[23] In TCA CROSS, a clinician applies a strong TCA solution point by point to individual scars, intending to stimulate new collagen in the scar base. Because the acid is confined to the scars, it is distinct from a full-face peel.[20]

A 2026 comprehensive review by Stratman and He covered 34 publications and 937 patients and reported improvement rates between 50 and 80 percent, with multiple sessions giving greater improvement and higher TCA concentrations raising complication risk. The most common adverse events were transient post-inflammatory pigment changes.[20] A 2026 scoping review of TCA for atrophic acne scars has also been published.[19]

sections.h: Comparisons with microneedling and other scar treatments
paras: A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis in Cureus pooled 11 studies and 713 participants comparing microneedling with chemical peels for atrophic acne scars. For clinically significant improvement (at least 50 percent) it found no significant difference (RR 0.97); for any improvement, microneedling was favoured (RR 1.79); and continuous severity scores showed no significant difference. Microneedling caused more procedural pain, while peels caused burning and exfoliation.[19]

A 2026 exploratory network meta-analysis of nine randomised trials found that combinations such as microneedling plus a chemical peel had numerically lower scar severity than laser alone, but all confidence intervals crossed the null and the authors rated confidence as low to very low.[19] A registered trial of microneedling with glycolic or trichloroacetic acid for atrophic acne scars (60 participants) and a trial of 35% TCA against intralesional saline (126 participants) have also been completed, without results listed in the registry.[24][25]

Melasma is a common, chronic and relapsing pigmentation disorder linked to UV exposure, hormones and genetics, and Wikipedia lists chemical peels among its procedures alongside topical regimens and sun protection.[22] Clinical trials in the TCA literature compare TCA with Jessner's solution, with ascorbic acid combinations and with glycolic acid, and a meta-analysis of single-agent peels in darker skin pooled 478 patients, finding glycolic acid favoured over TCA on the MASI score.[4][7][15]

A 2026 narrative review of noninvasive cosmetic treatments for Fitzpatrick skin types IV to VI states that superficial peels offer high satisfaction, that medium-depth peels need caution and that deep peels should be avoided in dark skin because of the risk of pigment change.[20] A 2026 scoping review of peels in skin of color screened 473 studies, included seven, and reported positive outcomes with minimal adverse effects in five acne and scarring studies and chemical burns from improper use in one.[21] A 2004 report described a focal TCA method for benign pigmented lesions in dark-skinned patients.[9]

A 2025 report in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology identified 18 skin injuries from layperson use of chemical peel products between August 2018 and August 2023, including burns, pain, swelling and scarring, some with disfiguring scars and reduced mobility; some products were labelled with concentrations typically used by healthcare professionals.[20] A 2026 paper in Anais Brasileiros de Dermatologia is titled as describing unpredictable behaviour and a risk of severe hypertrophic scarring with TCA-croton oil peels.[20]

Randomised 5-year trial in 34 veterans examined facial resurfacing for actinic keratoses and new skin cancers. [3] A comparative study of 30 women with epidermal melasma compared 20% TCA alone with TCA plus topical 5% ascorbic acid. [4] A randomised trial compared 35% TCA with 5-ALA photodynamic therapy for multiple actinic keratosis; a systematic review of field-cancerisation treatments noted clinical improvement favouring the photodynamic therapy. [5][17]

A pilot study of three men examined collagen changes after a single 35% TCA peel. [6] Registered trials compared TCA with salicylic acid for acne (n=60), with Jessner's solution for melasma, and with salicylic-azelaic combination for acne. [7][11][18]

Beyond these, a 2026 meta-analysis of 11 studies compared microneedling with chemical peels for atrophic acne scars,[19] and a review of TCA CROSS pooled 34 publications.[20] A registered trial of 15% TCA for hand lentigines (20 participants) has also been completed.[26]

Some forum members discuss doing TCA peels at home, a practice clinicians and the Wikipedia chemical peel article associate with injury and scarring risk; medium-depth peels are described there as procedures for a medical provider. [2]

lore.intro: Some forum members discuss applying TCA at home for acne scars or pigment, a practice the chemical peel literature associates with injury; the Wikipedia article states that medium-depth peels are intended for medical providers.[2][20]

claims.claim: A home TCA peel can smooth acne scars
claims.believers: Online skin-care communities describe applying TCA to scars or pigment themselves.[2]
claims.experts: Clinical TCA CROSS studies are performed by clinicians, and a 2025 report documented 18 layperson peel injuries including disfiguring scars.[20]

claims.claim: TCA is a strong option for acne scars
claims.believers: Proponents point to point-by-point scar treatment and multiple sessions.
claims.experts: A review of 34 publications reported 50 to 80 percent improvement rates, while a meta-analysis found no significant difference from microneedling for at least 50 percent improvement.[19][20]

claims.believers: Clinic-based peel protocols combine TCA with ascorbic acid or pretreatments.[4][8]
claims.experts: A pooled analysis found glycolic acid favoured over TCA on MASI, with other comparisons not significantly different.[15]

claims.claim: Medium-depth peels suit all skin tones
claims.believers: Some practitioners describe focal techniques that limit pigment change.[9]
claims.experts: A 2026 review advises caution with medium peels and avoiding deep peels in skin types IV to VI.[20]
